newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan ministry reprimands officials over DKB probe.
newsitem.headline: Japan ministry reprimands officials over DKB probe.

text.p: Japan's Finance Ministry said on Tuesday it had reprimanded two of its officials who conducted inspections of Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) for accepting favours from officials of the scandal-tainted firm.
DKB, one of Japan's top banks, is entangled along with giant Nomura Securities Co Ltd in a high-profile scandal involving payoffs to a "sokaiya" corporate racketeer.
A MOF official told reporters that two ministry officials assigned to inspect DKB in 1994 had been entertained with food and drinks by DKB officials and had also played golf with them.
He said the expenses for the entertainment had been paid by the bank, but did not specify how much money was involved.

Current Vice Finance Minister Takeshi Komura also received a written warning from the ministry as he headed the minister's secretariat at the time, a position in which he was partly responsible for overseeing the conduct of ministry officials.

MOF said the acts had not affected the results of the inspection but it was necessary to maintain discipline so that inspections would not lose social credibility. He said the two officials reprimanded had taken steps on Tuesday to reimburse DKB for the expenses.
The ministry came under fire when DKB's role in the scandal broke for failing to discover the dubious deals, although officials said it was virtually impossible to uncover what banks chose to hide.

More than a dozen people, including top executives from the DKB and Nomura, have been arrested in the affair, which coincides with the start of "Big Bang" reforms aimed at introducing more competition and global standards into Japan's long-sheltered financial sector.
DKB was fined 500,000 yen ($4,273) by Tokyo Summary Court on Monday for hiding loans to Ryuichi Koike, the "sokaiya" racketeer at the heart of the affair.

The fine, the maximum allowed under the Banking Law, followed a Finance Ministry complaint to prosecutors against the bank and four of its former officials alleging they had hidden information about problem loans to Koike during a ministry inspection in October 1994.
On Wednesday, the ministry is expected to announce administrative penalties against Nomura -- now embroiled in its second scandal in six years -- as well as DKB.

The financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun said on Tuesday that the ministry was likely to suspend Nomura's equity department from stock trading for its own account for four to five months and suspend business at the brokerage's corporate department for at least four months.
The newspaper also said the ministry would probably bar DKB from extending new loans and might also limit bond trading for its own account.
Payoffs to sokaiya have been illegal since 1993 but many Japanese companies have found it difficult to cut off ties with the underworld.

Sokaiya typically buy shares in companies and try to extort money from them by threatening to expose dubious business practices. Alternatively, they are sometimes employed by firms to quash questions from legitimate shareholders at annual meetings.
